question: You switch from 1024-token chunks to 256-token chunks and keep top-k at 2. What is the most likely new problem?
options: Each chunk's embedding becomes vaguer, so precision drops
The prompt overflows the context window
The LLM now sees a quarter as much text, so answers that span several sentences may lose a needed piece
Overlap stops working because it only applies to large chunks
explain: Smaller chunks give sharper embeddings, but 2 chunks of 256 tokens is 512 tokens of evidence instead of 2048. That is why the LlamaIndex example doubles top-k when it halves chunk size. Our toy shows the same thing: with 12-word chunks the 6 weeks chunk sits at rank 4.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: The seven failure points and how to debug them
question: A user asks for the refund policy as a bulleted list. The answer is correct and grounded but comes back as one paragraph. Which failure point is this?
options: FP5 Wrong Format
FP4 Not Extracted
FP7 Incomplete
FP2 Missed the Top Ranked Documents
explain: The facts are present and right; only the requested format was ignored. Barnett et al. define FP5 as the LLM ignoring an instruction to extract information in a certain format such as a table or list.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Document, query and interaction signals: freshness, popularity, clicks
question: Which feature is most likely to be inflated by position bias?
options: Title BM25
Query-URL click count
URL length
Document age
explain: Click counts depend on where the document was shown: top results get examined and clicked more even when a lower result is more relevant, as the swapped-order experiment showed. The other three do not depend on past rankings.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: nDCG precisely: gain, discount, log base and the ideal
question: A run's grade 3 document at rank 1 and grade 1 document at rank 4 swap places. Which raw DCG@5 variant drops more?
options: Linear gain, because it is proportional to the grade
Neither, because DCG ignores grades beyond binary relevance
Exponential gain, because it makes the grade 3 worth 7 instead of 3
They drop equally, because only the discounts change
explain: The swap costs (gain difference) x (1 - 0.431). Linear gain: 2 x 0.569 = 1.14. Exponential gain: (7 - 1) x 0.569 = 3.41. Exponential gain amplifies anything involving the top grade, which is why it is preferred when a few excellent results matter most.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? Paired tests, effect sizes, many systems
question: You compare 8 rankers pairwise with 28 independent paired t-tests at alpha = 0.05 and find 2 significant differences. What is the main concern?
options: With 28 tests, the chance of at least one false positive is about 0.76, so 2 hits are weak evidence; use ANOVA plus a multiple comparison test such as randomised Tukey HSD
The t-test cannot be used with paired data
The Wilcoxon test would have been more accurate
Nothing; each test is valid on its own
explain: 1 - 0.95^28 is about 0.76, so finding a couple of significant pairs is close to what chance alone would produce. Sakai suggests testing all systems together first and then applying a multiple comparison procedure. Smucker et al. found Wilcoxon less reliable, not more.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Memory registration: pinning, translation and keys
question: A cache server registers each 4 KB request buffer just before using it and deregisters it after. Throughput is poor. What is the best fix?
options: Use RDMA READ instead of WRITE
Register one large pool at startup, preferably on huge pages, and reuse buffers from it
Disable the protection domain
Use more QPs
explain: Registration enters the kernel and pins pages, so per-request registration puts the slow control path back on the data path. Registering a pool once fixes that, and large pages keep the NIC's translation cache small (FaRM's lesson).

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Scaling RDMA: NIC caches, doorbells, timeouts and failure
question: Your RC QP has `timeout = 14` and `retry_cnt = 7`. A peer machine loses power mid-transfer. What does the sender see, and roughly when?
options: Nothing; the WR stays pending forever
An IBV_WC_RETRY_EXC_ERR completion after on the order of half a second, with the QP in an error state
An RNR error immediately
A TCP reset
explain: With no ACKs, the NIC retries after each 67.1 ms timeout; once retry_cnt is exhausted the WR completes with IBV_WC_RETRY_EXC_ERR (about 8 x 67 ms = 537 ms in the simple model). RNR is about missing receive buffers on a live peer, not a dead one.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Delta-encoded state and choosing the transport
question: A Colyseus room has 200 entities and you call `sort()` on their ArraySchema every tick to keep a leaderboard ordered. Bandwidth spikes. Why?
options: Sorting changes refIds, which forces a full resync
Schemas cannot hold more than 63 entities
sort() marks every index as changed, so the whole array is re-sent every patch
Sorted arrays disable delta encoding for the whole room
explain: The Colyseus optimization docs: sort() re-sends every element because every index is marked changed. Sort a plain copy on the client, or sort a separate array of indexes, instead.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Implicit feedback: preference, confidence and weighted ALS
question: Why does the identity Y^T C^u Y = Y^T Y + Y^T (C^u - I) Y matter?
options: It makes the loss convex in X and Y jointly
It lets each user update cost depend on that user's n_u touched items instead of all n items, so a sweep is linear in the number of non-zeros
It removes the need for regularization
It turns ALS into SGD
explain: Y^T Y is shared and precomputed once per sweep. The user-specific correction only involves rows with c_ui different from 1, which are the items the user touched.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Why one pixels-per-mm ratio fails on a tilted photo
question: When is a single pixels-per-mm ratio from the card exact for an object on the same table?
options: Whenever the card and the object are both fully visible
When you average the ratios from all four edges
When the image plane is parallel to the table, so every table point has the same depth
When the object is shorter than the card
explain: With the camera looking straight at the plane, every point on it has the same Z, so f/Z is one constant. Averaging edges or keeping the object short reduces nothing about perspective; only a fronto-parallel view makes the ratio constant (ignoring lens distortion).

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: When each join wins: row counts, probes and memory
question: Which input should a hash join normally build its hash table on?
options: The larger input, so probing is cheaper
Whichever comes first in the FROM clause
The input that is already sorted
The smaller input, so the table fits in memory
explain: Build cost and memory grow with the build side, while each probe is a constant-time lookup either way. Building on the smaller input keeps the table in memory and avoids batching. In the docs' plan the Hash node sits over the 100-row tenk1 scan, not the 10000-row tenk2.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leaderless quorums: why R + W > N makes reads overlap writes
question: N = 5 with R = 4, W = 2. Reads always overlap the last write, yet two clients writing the same key at the same time can both succeed without either write reaching a replica that has the other. Why?
options: Because R + W = 6 is too close to N
Because W = 2 is not a majority of 5, so two write sets can be disjoint
Because reads with R = 4 cannot tolerate failures
Because coordinators send writes to only W replicas
explain: Read/write overlap needs R + W > N. Write/write overlap needs 2W > N. Two sets of 2 fit disjointly inside 5 replicas, so concurrent writers cannot detect each other through a shared replica.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When a high score stops meaning a solved task
question: Which of these is NOT reward hacking?
options: An agent edits the unit tests so they pass without fixing the bug
A robot moves between the camera and the object so a learned reward model thinks it grasped it
A model fails a coding task because it cannot write the algorithm, and gets reward 0
A boat circles to re-collect shaping points instead of finishing the race
explain: Reward hacking requires a high proxy score with poor true performance. A model that honestly fails gets a low proxy score that matches its true performance: that is a capability gap, not a specification failure.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: Catching hacks: CoT monitors, obfuscation, generalization
question: Your team's CoT monitor flags 5 percent of training rollouts as hacking. A teammate proposes subtracting reward whenever the monitor fires. Based on Baker et al., what is the main risk?
options: The monitor will become more accurate over time and over-penalize
GRPO cannot use non-binary rewards
After enough optimization the agent may keep hacking while writing CoTs that no longer reveal it, so the 5 percent signal drops without the hacking stopping
The model will stop producing a chain of thought
explain: In their experiment, the CoT-pressured agent hacked less early on but later hacked at a significant rate with monitor recall near zero. A falling flag rate would then look like success while hiding the problem. Using the monitor to find and patch environment bugs keeps the signal.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step
question: A disaggregated run broadcasts a 70B BF16 model (140 GB) from one trainer rank over a single 400 Gb/s NIC every step. Roughly how long is the transfer at line rate, and what is the cheapest big improvement?
options: 0.35 s; nothing to improve
2.8 s; send disjoint shards from many trainer ranks in parallel so many NICs carry the load
28 s; switch to FP32 to avoid conversions
280 s; checkpoint to shared storage instead
explain: 140 GB at 50 GB/s is 2.8 s. The transfer is limited by one NIC. Sending shards from many trainer ranks in parallel (8 NICs gives 0.35 s), shard-to-shard resharding, or overlapping the sync with generation all help; FP32 doubles the bytes.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Ceilings, hierarchical rooflines and Nsight Compute
question: Nsight Compute shows a kernel's L1, L2 and DRAM points almost on top of each other, sitting on the DRAM slope. What is the best next step?
options: Switch to Tensor Cores to raise the flat roof
Restructure for reuse (tiling, fusion) so fewer bytes reach DRAM
Nothing: being on the DRAM roof means it is already optimal
Raise the clock frequency to move the ridge point left
explain: Overlapping points mean almost every byte touched in L1 also came from DRAM: no reuse. The kernel is on the DRAM roof at its current intensity, so the way up is to raise intensity by reusing data in shared memory or registers, or by fusing with neighbors. A higher flat roof does nothing for a memory bound kernel.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: MTTR: detect, triage, mitigate, resolve
question: A team reduced detection from 8 minutes to 1 by alerting on every service's CPU, queue depth and pool wait. Their mean time to resolution got worse. What most likely happened?
options: Detection and triage are independent, so this cannot happen
More alerts means more deduplication work in Alertmanager, which delays notification
Cause-based alerts detect faster but page more often and from more places, so the alert storm grew and triage took longer than the detection saved
Alerting on saturation is always wrong
explain: Cause-based alerting trades triage time for detection time, and the trade is often bad: every service that is merely a victim now pages too. The SLO-based pattern is to page on the symptom your users feel and keep the cause-level signals as unpaged context, which is exactly what lesson 1 did with 9 groups and 1 page. Saturation signals are valuable; paging a human on each of them is the problem.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Ties, missing documents and the window size
question: Your fused results flicker between two orders on repeated identical requests. Which fix addresses the most likely cause?
options: Increase k
Add an explicit tie-break (best single rank, then document id) after sorting by RRF score
Normalize scores with min-max before RRF
Switch to CombSUM
explain: Exact RRF ties are frequent (any two documents with the same multiset of ranks). Without an explicit secondary key their order depends on hash or arrival order. Changing k changes which documents tie but does not remove ties.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Pinning: building kernel objects where they will live
question: Which struct field must be declared with `#[pin]` and initialized with `<-`?
options: `count: u64`
`name: &'static CStr`
`state: Mutex<State>`
`buf: KVec<u8>` (the vector's heap buffer may be reallocated)
explain: The `Mutex` wraps a C `struct mutex` that the kernel requires to stay at the address it was initialized at, so it is pinned and built in place with `new_mutex!`. A `KVec` may move its *buffer* on growth, but the KVec struct itself (pointer, length, capacity) can be moved freely.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
question: Your enqueue callback calls scx_bpf_dsq_insert_vtime(p, SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL, slice, vtime, flags). What happens?
options: Tasks are kept in vtime order inside the global DSQ
The vtime is ignored and the task is appended FIFO
It is an error: built-in DSQs do not support priority-queue insertion, so you need a custom DSQ
The task is silently moved to the caller CPU's local DSQ
explain: Built-in DSQs (local and global) are FIFO only. The docs and scx_simple's comments say vtime insertion needs a DSQ created with scx_bpf_create_dsq(); invalid use is reported as a scheduler error, which unloads it.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
question: After three rounds in the toy, move d has prior 0. Suppose d was actually the best move and its value estimate was wrong. What happens in later rounds without exploration noise?
options: d is never visited, because its exploration bonus is P(d) times something, which is 0, and its Q stays 0
800 simulations are enough that the search reaches d eventually
The value loss on z will raise P(d) automatically
The gate at 55% will reject the network and restore d
explain: The pUCT bonus is proportional to the prior. With P(d) = 0 and an unvisited Q of 0, d never has the highest score, so the search never looks at it and the outcome z never reflects it. This is exactly why AlphaZero adds Dirichlet noise to the root prior during self-play.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Inventing the tasks: Absolute Zero and what bounds every loop
question: A team wants a model to improve its customer-support replies, has thousands of real customer questions, and has no answer key or human preference labels. Which loop fits, and what is the main risk to monitor?
options: ReST-EM with a binary correctness reward; the risk is overfitting a small problem set
AlphaZero-style tree search; the risk is lack of exploration noise
Absolute Zero; the risk is nondeterministic programs
Self-Rewarding with the model as judge; the risk is the policy exploiting the judge, for example by growing longer replies
explain: Without checkable answers, the options are a judge or a human target. Self-Rewarding needs only prompts and a seed of judging examples. Its documented risk is that the judge's biases get amplified: the paper itself saw average response length grow about 2.3x over two iterations and flagged reward hacking.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Prompt compression: pruning tokens with a small language model
question: In the token-level example, keeping the top half of tokens dropped "pm" from "3 pm". Which change best fixes this?
options: Use a larger percentile so fewer tokens are kept
Score and filter phrase-level units, so "3 pm" is kept or dropped as a whole
Use a bigger target LLM
Drop the most surprising tokens instead
explain: "pm" is predictable once you have seen "3", so it has little self-information on its own, yet the unit "3 pm" carries the meaning. Selective Context merges tokens into phrases or sentences for this reason, and LLMLingua's budget controller likewise works at coarser levels first.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Inside the server: three processes and an overlapped loop
question: Why can't the scheduler simply build batch k+1 while batch k runs, with no extra machinery?
options: Batch k+1 needs batch k's sampled tokens as its inputs, which are not known until batch k finishes; SGLang uses future-token placeholders resolved on the GPU
The GPU cannot run two kernels in a row
Python cannot start a second thread
The radix tree must be rebuilt from scratch every step
explain: For decoding, each step's input is the previous step's output. Overlap therefore needs a way to refer to tokens that do not exist yet. The release notes describe resolving this dependency with future tokens and careful CUDA event synchronization.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: A*: steering the search with a lower bound
question: To speed things up, someone divides straight-line km by 30 km/h instead of the network's top speed of 60 km/h. What is the risk?
options: None; any distance-based estimate keeps A* optimal
A* will settle more nodes than before
The heuristic may now overestimate on fast roads, so A* can return a slower route than the optimum
The algorithm may loop forever
explain: At 30 km/h each kilometer is estimated at 2 minutes, but a 60 km/h road covers it in 1. Overestimating breaks Theorem 1's condition, so optimality is no longer guaranteed. The survey notes such aggressive bounds speed things up only by giving up correctness.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: Frequency bins, resolution and spectral leakage
question: You record 2 s of data at 1000 Hz and need to tell apart tones at 50.0 Hz and 50.3 Hz. What helps?
options: Zero-pad to 8 times the length before the FFT
Sample at 4000 Hz instead of 1000 Hz for the same 2 s
Record for longer: at least several seconds, since the bin spacing is 1/duration
Apply a Hann window, which sharpens peaks
explain: Resolution is fs/N = 1/duration. Two seconds gives 0.5 Hz bins, too coarse for a 0.3 Hz gap; you need more than 1/0.3 = 3.3 s, and more still with a window, which widens peaks. A higher fs adds bins at high frequencies but keeps the spacing at 1/duration. Zero-padding only interpolates the same blurred spectrum.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Writing a vector loop: intrinsics, reductions and tails
question: You remove the scalar tail loop from sum_avx2 to save code. What happens for n = 19?
options: Nothing, the vector loop reads all 19 elements
It returns 136, silently dropping a[16], a[17] and a[18]
It crashes because the last load is out of bounds
It returns 190 but more slowly
explain: The vector loop stops at i = 16 because 16 + 8 > 19, so it never reads past the end. Without the tail the last 3 elements are never added: you get 136 instead of 190. Silent wrong answers like this are the classic SIMD bug.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Shipping SIMD: -march levels, runtime dispatch, portability
question: You ship a desktop app built with `-march=x86-64-v4` because benchmarks on your AVX-512 workstation looked great. Users with AVX2-only laptops report crashes at startup. What is the right fix?
options: Add -O3
Build for the baseline or x86-64-v3 and use target_clones or runtime checks for the AVX-512 hot loops
Switch to -ffast-math
Catch SIGILL and retry
explain: x86-64-v4 lets the compiler place AVX-512 instructions anywhere, including startup code. Build the bulk for a level every user has, and multiversion only the hot kernels so each CPU picks its best copy.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: The slab allocator: caches of ready-made objects
question: A slab holds 31 objects of 128 bytes in a 4096-byte page, with 32 bytes of in-page metadata. Without coloring, every slab's objects start at offset 0. What does coloring change?
options: It fits a 32nd object into the page by moving the metadata elsewhere
It uses the 96 leftover bytes to start each new slab's objects at a different offset, so hot fields of objects in different slabs map to different cache sets
It rounds the objects up to 256 bytes so each one is cache-line aligned
It marks freed objects with a pattern so use-after-free is detected
explain: 31 x 128 = 3968 bytes, plus 32 metadata leaves 96 spare bytes. Coloring spends that otherwise wasted space on an offset that varies per slab. (Filling freed memory with 0xdeadbeef is a separate debugging feature.)

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Moving weights from Megatron into SGLang
question: You move a working colocated job to separate pools and add `--update-weight-mode delta` but keep the default transport. What happens?
options: It fails an assertion: delta mode requires `--update-weight-transport disk`
It runs, shipping deltas over NCCL
It silently falls back to full NCCL sync
It uses CUDA IPC because the engines are on the same nodes
explain: `create_weight_updater` asserts that delta mode uses disk transport (and is not colocated). Delta sync works by publishing versioned checkpoint directories that engines pull, not by broadcasting.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Why single neurons are hard to read: superposition
question: In the pentagon model, which input is decoded wrongly with b = -0.309?
options: Only f1 on
f1 and f2 on (neighbours)
f1 and f3 on (non-neighbours)
No feature on
explain: Non-neighbours have cosine -0.809, so their sum cancels most of each one's own signal (0.191 each) while the shared neighbour f2 gets 0.618. After the bias only f2 survives. Neighbours reinforce each other instead.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features
question: Why does the Scaling Monosemanticity steering recipe keep the SAE error term instead of feeding the edited reconstruction alone into later layers?
options: To make the latent's activation non-negative
Because the error term is always zero for TopK SAEs
So the only change to the activation is the chosen feature; dropping the error would also remove everything the SAE fails to reconstruct
To reduce memory use
explain: Replacing x with the reconstruction alone would apply two edits at once: the feature clamp and the loss of all unexplained structure. Keeping the error makes x' = x + (c - f_i) d_i.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in map coordinates
question: Two estimates at the same point: simple kriging with an assumed mean of 13.0 gives 15.090; ordinary kriging gives 15.099. Why do they differ slightly?
options: Ordinary kriging uses a different variogram
Simple kriging ignores the nearest sensor
Simple kriging's weights need not sum to 1, so the assumed mean gets weight 1 minus their sum; ordinary kriging estimates the mean from the data instead
They are numerically unstable; the difference is rounding error
explain: Simple kriging writes the estimate as $m + \sum \lambda_i (z_i - m)$, so the known mean carries the leftover weight (here $1 - 1.042$). Ordinary kriging forces the weights to sum to 1, which is equivalent to using a data-estimated mean (12.80 here).

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Speculative sampling: guesses that keep the target's distribution
question: A teammate 'simplifies' the sampler: on rejection, sample the replacement from p instead of the residual. What happens?
options: Nothing; p and the residual are the same distribution
Outputs become biased toward tokens the draft under-proposes, because their accepted mass is counted twice
Outputs become biased toward tokens the draft over-proposes
Acceptance rate drops but outputs stay exact
explain: Rejection still happens with probability 0.3 in the toy example, but the replacement now follows p, so each token gets min(p, q) + 0.3 p(x): 0.45, 0.26, 0.16, 0.13 instead of 0.5, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1. 'a' and 'dog', which the draft over-proposes, gain mass. The residual sends rejected mass only to under-covered tokens, adding exactly the missing p(x) - q(x).

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: From 16,000 samples a second to a log-mel spectrogram
question: On the Slaney mel scale, which span covers more mel units: 0 to 1000 Hz or 4000 to 8000 Hz?
options: 0 to 1000 Hz (15 mel versus about 10.1 mel)
4000 to 8000 Hz, because it is four times wider in Hz
They are equal, because the scale is logarithmic everywhere
It depends on the number of mel bands
explain: 0 to 1000 Hz is the linear part: 15 mel. 4000 to 8000 Hz is one doubling in the log region: 27 ln 2 / ln 6.4, about 10.1 mel. So the filterbank spends more bands on the lowest kilohertz, where vowels and pitch live, than on the top four kilohertz. The number of bands only decides how finely the axis is cut.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Long audio, streaming and hallucinations in production
question: Window 1 predicts its last complete segment ends at 28.00 s, but the speaker actually finished it at 27.40 s and started a new sentence. What does buffered long-form transcription do next?
options: Starts window 2 at 30.00 s, as always
Starts window 2 at 28.00 s and may skip the words spoken between 27.40 and 28.00 s
Re-runs window 1 with a higher temperature
Averages the two timestamps and starts at 27.70 s
explain: The seek position follows the predicted timestamp, so window 2 starts at 28.00 s and the 600 ms after the true boundary is never transcribed. This is the error propagation between windows that the paper warns about.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Page faults: lazy allocation, copy-on-write and overcommit
question: A machine has 16 GiB of RAM, no swap and `vm.overcommit_memory = 0`. Processes A and B each malloc 12 GiB and each writes only its first 1 GiB. What most likely happens?
options: B's malloc returns NULL because 24 GiB exceeds RAM
Both mallocs succeed and both run normally: only touched pages use RAM
Both succeed, then the OOM killer immediately kills one of them
The kernel zeroes 24 GiB at malloc time and the machine swaps
explain: The default heuristic only rejects a single request bigger than RAM plus swap; 12 GiB is not, and it does not add up other processes' reservations. Frames are allocated on first touch, so about 2 GiB of RAM is used. Only if A and B actually wrote more than RAM holds would the OOM killer step in.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Side effects and how to evaluate a steering vector
question: A team builds a sycophancy vector from 500 A/B pairs, picks the layer and coefficient that maximize the score on those same 500 pairs, and reports a large effect. What is the main flaw?
options: They should have used fewer pairs
Sycophancy cannot be represented linearly
They should have reported MMLU instead of the behavior score
The vector, the hyperparameters and the reported score all come from the same data, so the effect is likely overstated; it needs held-out validation and test splits
explain: Choosing layer and c on the evaluation data overfits them to it. CAA scores on 50 held-out questions, ITI uses 2-fold cross-validation, and Arditi et al. keep train, validation and evaluation sets pairwise disjoint. Capability checks are needed too, but they do not fix the leak.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Windows, watermarks and allowed lateness, step by step
question: A Flink job reads a Kafka topic with 8 partitions. One partition stops receiving data. Per-minute windows stop producing results for all sensors. Why?
options: Kafka blocks all partitions when one is empty
Allowed lateness is too large
Tumbling windows require data in every partition
The operator's watermark is the minimum over its inputs, and the idle partition's watermark never advances
explain: Watermarks are tracked per partition and combined with a minimum. A silent partition pins the minimum, so no window end is ever passed. Marking idle inputs (withIdleness) lets the watermark advance without them.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Causal masks, cross-attention and multiple heads
question: In encoder-decoder (cross) attention, where do the queries, keys and values come from?
options: Queries, keys and values all come from the encoder output
Queries from the encoder; keys and values from the decoder
Queries from the decoder; keys and values from the encoder output
Queries and keys from the decoder; values from the encoder
explain: The decoder is asking questions about the source, so it supplies the queries. The encoder output supplies the keys (what each source position offers) and the values (what gets copied). This lets every decoder position attend over all input positions.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Why raw TF-IDF ranks a keyword-stuffed page first
question: Why does the long document C score high under TF-IDF even though it is not more focused on the query?
options: Its IDF values are higher
TF-IDF divides by document length, which favors long documents
C contains both query terms, and TF-IDF only scores documents with all terms
Longer documents have more tokens, so their raw counts are larger for many terms
explain: IDF depends only on the term, not the document. TF-IDF as written does not divide by length at all, and it scores any document with at least one term (A, B and D are scored too). C wins because a 60-token document simply has room for more occurrences.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Next-token prediction: turning raw text into training examples
question: A teammate's first logged loss on the 65-character model is 27. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The model is already overfitting
The data loader is shifting targets by two
The initialization makes some logits huge, so the model is confidently wrong
Nothing: 27 is typical for an untrained character model
explain: An untrained model with small weights should print about ln 65 = 4.17. A much larger loss means a very low probability on the true token, which only happens when logits are large and spread out, typically from weights initialized with too large a scale.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature and top-k
question: Why does generate keep only `logits[:, -1, :]`?
options: Earlier positions' logits are always wrong
It saves memory and gives the same result as averaging all positions
Only the last position's logits predict the token that comes after the current context
The causal mask zeroes out the other positions' logits
explain: Position t's logits predict token t+1. Earlier positions predict tokens that already exist in the context, so they are useless here. The causal mask zeroes attention weights, not logits.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backpropagation: the chain rule run backward through a graph
question: A model has 1 million parameters. Roughly how many forward evaluations of the loss does a centered finite-difference gradient need, compared with backprop?
options: About 2, the same as backprop
About 2 million, versus one forward plus one backward pass for backprop
About 1000, the square root of the parameter count
Exactly 1 million, versus 1 million backward passes for backprop
explain: Centered differences need two evaluations per parameter, $2 \times 10^6$ forward passes. Reverse-mode differentiation gets the whole gradient of a scalar loss from one forward and one backward pass, which is why finite differences are only used to spot-check gradients.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: Pipes: concurrent processes, sort | uniq -c, and SIGPIPE
question: Which pipeline lists the 3 most common words in words.txt (one word per line)?
options: `uniq -c words.txt | sort -rn | head -n 3`
`sort words.txt | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3`
`sort -rn words.txt | uniq -c | head -n 3`
`sort words.txt | head -n 3 | uniq -c`
explain: Sort first so equal words are adjacent, count with uniq -c, then sort the counts numerically in reverse and take 3. The third option sorts the words themselves, not counts, and the last one cuts the data before counting.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Negative sampling: one word2vec update by hand
question: Why is SGNS so much cheaper per training pair than the full softmax?
options: It uses smaller vectors
It skips the input vector update
It only trains on frequent words
It touches $k + 1$ output vectors instead of all $W$
explain: The softmax normalizer needs every output vector; the negative sampling objective needs only the true context and the k samples. With k = 5 and W = 1,000,000 that is 6 dot products instead of a million.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token
question: A 13B-parameter FP16 model runs on the same A100 at batch 1. Roughly what is the best-case decode speed?
options: About 78 tokens/s
About 152 tokens/s, the same as 7B
About 24,000 tokens/s
It depends only on the prompt length
explain: Weights are 26 GB; 26 GB / 2.039 TB/s is about 12.8 ms per token, or about 78 tokens/s. Decode time scales with bytes read, so twice the parameters means roughly half the speed.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The CPU loop: fetch, decode, execute, repeat
question: In `addq (%rdi,%rcx,8), %rax`, why is rcx multiplied by 8?
options: Because x86-64 has 8 general-purpose registers
Because the loop is unrolled 8 times
Because memory is read in 8-bit units
Because each long is 8 bytes, so element i starts 8 x i bytes after a
explain: Memory is addressed in bytes, and a long is 8 bytes on x86-64 Linux. a[i] therefore lives at address a + 8 x i. The CPU computes that address as part of the instruction (base rdi plus index rcx times scale 8).

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: every process gets its own addresses
question: Why does x86-64 use a 4-level tree instead of one flat table indexed by the 36-bit page number?
options: A flat table cannot be cached in the TLB
Flat tables cannot hold physical frame numbers
Hardware cannot index arrays larger than 512 entries
A flat table would need 2^36 entries x 8 bytes = 512 GiB per process, mostly describing unused memory
explain: 2^36 x 8 bytes = 512 GiB, for every process. A tree only allocates the lower-level tables for regions actually in use, so a small process needs a few pages of page tables. The cost is the longer walk, which the TLB hides.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward models: turning human comparisons into a score
question: Rewards are A = 2.0 and B = 1.0, and the human preferred B. What is the loss on this pair?
explain: The winner is B, so the gap is 1.0 - 2.0 = -1. Loss = -ln sigma(-1) = ln(1 + e) = 1.313. A wrongly ordered pair costs much more than ln 2.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Building the index: tokens, sorting and postings
question: After indexing, which statistic for a term equals the length of its postings list?
options: Its collection frequency
Its document frequency
Its largest term frequency
The number of positions stored for it
explain: One posting per document that contains the term, so the list length is df. Collection frequency counts every occurrence, which is the sum of the tf values stored in those postings.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Inverted indexes in real engines: compression, updates, Lucene
question: Why does Lucene add documents by writing new segments instead of inserting postings into existing lists?
options: Segments are needed to compute idf
Postings are compressed contiguous runs, so in-place insertion would mean rewriting them; append-only segments plus background merges avoid that
Each segment can only hold one field
Lucene cannot store more than 128 documents per segment
explain: Compressed, gap-encoded postings cannot absorb an insert cheaply. Writing a fresh small segment is fast, and merges later rewrite several segments into one larger, well-compressed segment. This is the same main plus auxiliary idea from the textbook, generalized to many segments. The 128 is the packed block size, not a segment limit.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Object lifetimes: automatic, static and malloc'd memory
question: After `free(p);` the program later runs `free(p);` again. What does the C standard say happens?
options: The second call does nothing, like free(NULL)
The behavior is undefined
free returns an error code
The memory is freed twice, which is harmless
explain: free on a block that has already been deallocated is explicitly undefined behavior. Only a null pointer is a guaranteed no-op, which is why some code writes `free(p); p = NULL;`.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Borrowing: many readers or one writer
question: Which snippet compiles?
options: `let a = &mut s; let b = &mut s; a.push('x'); b.push('y');`
`let a = &s; s.push('x'); println!("{a}");`
`let a = &mut s; a.push('x'); let b = &mut s; b.push('y');`
`let a = &s; let b = &mut s; println!("{a}{b}");`
explain: In option 3, `a` is last used before `b` is created, so the two mutable borrows do not overlap. Option 1 is E0499 (two live `&mut`). Options 2 and 4 are E0502 (a shared borrow is still used after a mutable one starts).

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A vector is a list of numbers and an arrow at the same time
question: You store 1,000 user profiles, each with 32 numeric features, as vectors. Which statement is right?
options: Each profile is a vector in R^1000
You cannot add two profiles because their features have different meanings
Each profile is a vector in R^32, and you can add two profiles component by component
Each feature is a vector in R^32
explain: Each profile has 32 components, so it lives in $\mathbb{R}^{32}$. The math allows adding any two vectors of the same dimension; whether the sum is *meaningful* depends on the features, but averaging profiles (add, then scale by 1/2) is a common and legal operation.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Where it shows up: linear layers, batches and attention scores
question: A colleague removes the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ factor and raises $d_k$ from 64 to 1024. What do you expect?
options: Nothing changes, because softmax only depends on the ranking of scores
Scores shrink toward 0, so attention becomes uniform
Scores spread about 4 times wider, softmax gets much peakier and training can slow because gradients shrink
The product QK^T becomes undefined
explain: Typical score size grows like $\sqrt{d_k}$: $\sqrt{1024}/\sqrt{64} = 4$. Softmax depends on score *differences*, not just their ranking, so wider scores mean near one-hot weights and tiny gradients. Shapes still match, so nothing errors.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Fighting overfitting: validation, weight decay, early stopping
question: Training loss keeps decreasing, while validation loss has risen for the last 20 epochs. Which action matches early stopping?
options: Keep training until training loss reaches zero
Raise the learning rate so the model escapes
Restore the parameters saved at the lowest validation loss and stop
Shrink the validation set so its loss is less noisy
explain: Early stopping keeps a copy of the best-validation parameters and returns them once validation stops improving. Continuing only widens the train/validation gap.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backpropagation through a whole network, by hand
question: A colleague implements BP2 as `d1 = (W2 @ d2) * a1 * (1 - a1)` for a network where W2 has shape (10, 64). What happens?
options: It works, matrix order does not matter
It computes the gradient for the biases instead
It fails or computes garbage: the error must go back through the transpose, W2.T @ d2, giving one value per hidden unit
It only breaks when the batch size is 1
explain: W2 maps 64 hidden units to 10 outputs. Going backward, the 10 output errors must be distributed to 64 hidden units along the same connections: that is $(W^2)^\top \delta^2$, shape 64. W2 @ d2 is a shape error here, and for square matrices it silently produces wrong gradients, which a gradient check would catch.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency: race conditions and locks
question: Why does the flag-based lock fail while the test-and-set lock works?
options: Test-and-set is faster, so the window for an interrupt is smaller
The flag lock forgets to reset the flag in unlock()
The flag lock only fails on multiprocessors
Test-and-set reads the old value and writes the new one as one atomic step, so two threads cannot both see the lock as free
explain: In the flag lock, a thread can test (see 0) and then be preempted before it sets the flag, letting another thread also see 0. Test-and-set fuses test and set into a single atomic operation. Speed has nothing to do with it, and the failure happens even on one CPU with a timer interrupt.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Random variables, expected value and variance
question: An LLM eval has 200 independent questions and the model answers each correctly with probability 0.7. What are the mean and standard deviation of the number correct?
options: Mean 140, standard deviation 42
Mean 140, standard deviation about 6.5
Mean 0.7, standard deviation 0.21
Mean 140, standard deviation 0.46
explain: Binomial with n = 200, p = 0.7: mean np = 140, variance np(1 - p) = 42, so the standard deviation is the square root, about 6.48. Option A forgets the square root. Runs of the same eval can differ by several questions from noise alone.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Why loss falls on a straight line in log-log space
question: A run at 100M non-embedding parameters reaches the loss Kaplan's fit predicts (2.83). Using the same law with ample data, what loss should a 10B model reach?
options: About 2.38
About 1.42, half the loss for 100x the size
About 1.99
About 2.83 minus 2 x 0.45, so 1.92
explain: Two 10x steps, each multiplying loss by 0.839: $2.83 \times 0.839^2 \approx 1.99$. 2.38 is only one step (1B). Subtracting a fixed amount per step assumes a linear trend, and halving would need about 9,139x more parameters, not 100x.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Inference cost, overtraining and where scaling laws break
question: A team will serve its model to millions of users for a year and needs a fixed quality bar. What does inference-aware scaling recommend?
options: Train the Chinchilla-optimal model, since it reaches the bar with the least compute
Train a smaller model on more tokens than Chinchilla-optimal, paying extra training compute to cut serving cost
Train the largest model the budget allows on fewer tokens, since bigger models are more sample-efficient
Train any size; inference cost does not depend on model size
explain: Serving costs about 2N FLOPs per token, so with heavy usage a smaller model that reaches the same loss by training longer has lower lifetime cost. Chinchilla-optimal minimizes training compute only. Bigger-and-shorter is Kaplan's advice and makes serving more expensive.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Comparing systems honestly: judgment holes, variance, online tests
question: B beats A on MAP, 0.43 versus 0.37, over 8 queries. B wins on 2 queries and loses on 6. Which conclusion is justified?
options: B is better: MAP is the standard measure
Not established yet: check per-query differences with a paired test and add queries
A is better because it wins more queries
They are identical because 8 queries is too few to compute MAP
explain: A mean driven by one or two queries is fragile, and with 8 queries neither a t-test (p = 0.44) nor a sign test (p = 0.29) supports a general claim. Counting wins alone is also not a valid conclusion. Use more queries (about 50 is a common minimum) and a paired test.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Where dense retrieval fails: hybrid search and re-ranking
question: A dense-only search works well on natural questions but users complain that searching an exact SKU like `KX-4471-B` returns similar-looking but wrong products. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Increase the embedding dimension from 384 to 1024
Lower the softmax temperature at query time
Switch from cosine to dot product
Add BM25 in parallel and fuse the lists with RRF
explain: Rare exact identifiers are where lexical matching is strongest and dense vectors are weakest. Hybrid retrieval keeps the dense model's paraphrase handling and adds exact-term recall. Temperature is a training-time setting; more dimensions or another similarity function do not create exact-match behavior.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Byte-level BPE: how GPT-2 and its successors tokenize anything
question: Why can GPT-2's tokenizer encode an emoji it never saw during tokenizer training, without an unknown token?
options: It has a fallback table of every Unicode character
The regex deletes characters it does not recognise
It maps any unseen character to the nearest known one
The emoji is UTF-8 bytes, and all 256 byte values are base tokens, so it can always be written as bytes
explain: The base vocabulary is the 256 byte values. Any string, emoji included, is a sequence of UTF-8 bytes, so in the worst case each byte is its own token. Merges only make common byte sequences shorter.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Learning rate: the stability limit, warmup, decay and clipping
question: Your loss is fine for 200 steps, then spikes to NaN. Halving the learning rate fixes it, but training is now slow. Which change best addresses the cause while keeping speed?
options: Add linear warmup and global-norm gradient clipping, then return to the original peak learning rate
Increase the batch size without changing the learning rate
Switch the cosine decay to a constant learning rate
Lower the momentum to 0
explain: A late spike at an otherwise good learning rate points to occasional oversized steps. Clipping caps those rare steps without slowing ordinary ones, and warmup keeps the early, high-curvature phase stable. Halving the rate everywhere pays the cost on every step.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Greedy search on a proximity graph, and why ef matters
question: On the toy graph, greedy search (ef = 1) returned F instead of H. Which change would most directly let it find H?
options: Start from F instead of A
Use cosine distance instead of Euclidean
Remove the edge between D and F
Raise ef so G is kept in the result list
explain: With ef = 3, G (3.0) survives in W after D is expanded, and expanding G reveals H. Changing the start node or edges is not something you control per query; ef is the query-time knob.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: The Gaussian loop: unbiased fits that still shrink to a point
question: Which statement about the M = 10 loop is correct?
options: The expected variance falls each generation, so the estimator is biased
The typical variance stays near 1, but the expected variance collapses
The expected variance stays at 1, but the typical (median) run collapses toward 0
Both the expected and typical variance stay near 1
explain: Unbiasedness makes the variance a martingale, so its expectation is 1 forever. The median follows the drift of the log and collapses. A heavy right tail of rare runs keeps the mean at 1.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What happens when your program calls write
question: mmap returns a pointer. The raw syscall can also fail. How does libc tell a valid address from an error in rax?
options: A valid address is never negative, so any value with the top bit set is an error
The kernel sets the carry flag on error
Values from -4095 to -1 (the top 4095 addresses) are reserved for errors; anything else is a result
mmap returns 0 on error
explain: On x86-64 Linux there is no separate error flag (the syscall(2) table lists none). Those top 4095 values lie in the kernel half of the address space, never a user mapping, so glibc treats raw results in that range as negated error codes. A user-space mapping address is a normal positive number, but checking the top bit alone would be wrong in general.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Fan-out: why one server's p99 becomes everyone's problem
question: Why does fan-out make tail latency matter more than median latency for the user?
options: Because the root averages the leaf latencies, and averages are dominated by outliers
Because leaves process requests serially
Because the user waits for the slowest of N responses, so a rare per-leaf event becomes a common per-request event
Because median latency cannot be measured at the root
explain: The root waits for the maximum, not the mean, of the leaf latencies. The probability that the maximum includes a tail event grows as 1 - (1-p)^N.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Why summing job durations overstates experience
question: A candidate has two roles: Jan 2020 to Dec 2022 full-time and Jan 2021 to Dec 2021 part-time (both inclusive). A filter asks for 4+ years of experience. What should happen?
options: Match: 36 + 12 = 48 months is exactly 4 years
No match: the union is 36 months, 3 years
Match, because part-time roles always count double
It cannot be decided without the LLM
explain: The part-time role lies entirely inside the full-time one, so the union is Jan 2020 to Dec 2022, 36 months. Summing gives 48 months only because 2021 is counted twice.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Let the LLM parse and let code do the date math
question: Why does `date(2023, 1, 31) + relativedelta(months=1)` return 2023-02-28 instead of raising an error or returning March 3?
options: relativedelta clamps to the last valid day: adding months never crosses a month boundary
It adds 28 days
It converts the date to a timestamp and adds 30 days
February 29 is skipped in non-leap years by adding 29 days
explain: The dateutil docs state that adding a month never crosses the month boundary, so day 31 is clamped to the last day of February. That is the calendar-month semantics you want for *Sep 2021 plus 3 years* style questions.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Search against a PRM, revisions, and compute-optimal allocation
question: A product mostly receives easy prompts that the model already solves 70% of the time. Which allocation does the paper's evidence favor?
options: Deep lookahead search against a PRM
Spend the budget sequentially (revise or keep reasoning) rather than on aggressive PRM search
Skip any verifier and return the first sample
Always use the maximum number of parallel samples
explain: On easy bins, sequential revisions did best and beam search degraded with budget. Light selection (vote or weighted best-of-N) over a revision chain is the safer choice.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: One gradient step on a key-value loss is the delta rule
question: Which pair of choices turns the generic TTT layer into plain linear attention?
options: Linear model, batch gradient descent, W_0 = 0
Linear model, online gradient descent, W_0 = 0
Two-layer MLP, batch gradient descent, learned W_0
Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression with a softmax kernel
explain: Theorem 1 of the TTT paper: linear model, batch GD (all gradients at W_0) and W_0 = 0 give linear attention. Online GD gives the delta rule instead. The kernel-regression option is Theorem 2, which recovers softmax attention, not linear attention.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: One lock, many cores: why a shared slab cache stops scaling
question: Why did the original slab allocator get *slower* in total when going from 1 to 16 threads, rather than just staying flat?
options: Each thread ran its constructors twice
Contention made each lock handoff more expensive (cache line transfers, waiting, wakeups), so the serialized work itself took longer
The Starfire had only one memory controller
The slab layer disabled interrupts
explain: A flat ceiling assumes the critical section costs the same under load. Under contention the lock and freelist lines move between CPUs on every acquisition and waiters spin or sleep, so each serialized operation gets slower. The paper calls this increasingly pathological lock contention.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Today: thread caches, per-CPU caches and restartable sequences
question: In TCMalloc's rseq push (free), the code writes the object pointer into the slot and then stores the incremented `current`. Why is it fine if the thread is preempted between those two stores?
options: Preemption is disabled during free
The slot write is atomic
Nothing is published until the store to current commits; a restarted sequence just overwrites the same slot
The kernel replays the first store for it
explain: Only the final store to `current` makes the new object visible. If the thread is interrupted after writing the slot but before committing, the sequence restarts, recomputes the slot from the current header and rewrites it. TCMalloc's rseq notes describe exactly this: preempted sequences overwrite the deallocated object until one commits.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: The SSD tier, zswap, and running tiering in production
question: DRAM holds a job's hot pages and CXL is full of warm pages touched every few seconds. Another 50 GB of pages are touched about once per hour. Where should those 50 GB go?
options: SSD swap (with zswap in front): one major fault per page per hour is negligible
Move warm CXL pages to SSD swap so the hourly pages fit on CXL
DRAM, by demoting some hot pages to CXL
Nowhere: tiering cannot help this job
explain: Cost is access rate times miss cost. An hourly page pays one 10 to 40 us fault per hour, which is nothing; a warm page on swap would fault every few seconds. The coldest pages belong in the lowest tier.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Prophet, the M4 competition and foundation models
question: What does zero-shot forecasting with Chronos mean?
options: Forecasting with zero horizon
Forecasting a series the model was not trained on, without fitting to it
Training on zero-valued series only
Using no seasonal component
explain: Chronos is pretrained on a large corpus. Zero-shot means applying it directly to a new series with no training on that dataset. The Chronos paper reports comparable and occasionally better accuracy than models trained on those datasets.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Tiled matmul: 2D pointer blocks, tl.dot and grouped ordering
question: A colleague removes other=0.0 from the A and B loads in the K loop because "the C store is masked anyway". When does this break?
options: Never, the store mask covers it
Only when M is not a multiple of BLOCK_SIZE_M
When K is not a multiple of BLOCK_SIZE_K, because undefined values in the last K tile get summed into every output
Only on AMD GPUs
explain: The store mask only drops rows and columns outside C. Garbage in the K dimension is not outside C: it is multiplied and accumulated into valid outputs. Masked K lanes must load 0.0, the neutral element of the sum in the dot product.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Attention masks for mixed text and image sequences
question: Why can Transfusion open up attention inside the image when Chameleon cannot?
options: Transfusion uses a larger context window
Chameleon images are smaller
Transfusion denoises all patches of an image at once, so every patch exists at every step, whereas Chameleon emits patches one by one
Transfusion has no text tokens inside images
explain: In a diffusion step all n patches (noisy versions of them) are in the sequence simultaneously, so a patch attending to a later patch reads something real. In token-by-token generation a later patch has not been sampled yet, so letting an earlier one see it during training would be a leak.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Building the image: micro-libraries, configuration and dead code
question: A unikernel serves files only from a RAM filesystem. Why does its image contain no block device driver, even though the Unikraft source tree has one?
options: The hypervisor provides block storage, so the driver is never needed
Block drivers are loaded as kernel modules at boot
Only components selected in the configuration or pulled in as dependencies are compiled and linked; nothing references the block layer
Dead code elimination removes all drivers by default
explain: Unikraft builds only selected micro-libraries and their dependencies. The paper notes the nginx image has no block subsystem because it only uses RamFS. There are no loadable modules in a unikernel.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Why one vector distance is mostly a memory problem
question: Squared L2 has intensity 0.75 FLOP per byte and dot product 0.5. On a memory-bound scan, which runs faster per distance?
options: Dot product, because it does fewer FLOPs
About the same, because both read the same 4d bytes
L2, because higher intensity is always faster
Neither can be computed with SIMD
explain: When the limit is bytes, the extra subtract in L2 hides under the memory stall. Both read one 3,072-byte vector per distance, so their throughput is about equal.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Why verl splits the RL loop from the GPU programs
question: Why doesn't HybridFlow simply use a single controller for everything, as classic RL frameworks such as RLlib do?
options: Single controllers cannot express data dependencies between models
Ray does not support GPU workers
Dispatching every operation of a sharded LLM from one central process adds too much overhead; SPMD inside each model avoids it
A single controller forces all models to use the same parallelism
explain: The paper's diagnosis: single-controller frameworks were built for networks of at most hundreds of MB. For LLMs with complex parallelism the central dispatch overhead is too high, so HybridFlow keeps central control only between nodes and lets each node run multi-controller.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Backends, placement and running verl in practice
question: A colocated run trains fine but crashes with out-of-memory right when the first rollout starts after an update. Which setting is the most likely culprit?
options: rollout.gpu_memory_utilization is set too high for GPUs that also hold training state
data.train_batch_size is not divisible by the number of GPUs
algorithm.adv_estimator is set to grpo
trainer.balance_batch is enabled
explain: At the transition the rollout reclaims its weight and KV cache memory on GPUs where the training engine may still hold parameters or optimizer state. For vLLM, gpu_memory_utilization is a fraction of total memory, so a value that ignores the colocated trainer overcommits. Lowering it or enabling offload addresses the transition.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Merging similar frames: MovieChat and MA-LMM memory banks
question: Why do MovieChat and MA-LMM only merge temporally adjacent frames instead of the globally most similar pair?
options: Global similarity is impossible to compute
Adjacent merging keeps temporal order, so each merged token still stands for one contiguous stretch of time
Adjacent frames are always identical
It makes the LLM context longer
explain: If the speaker returns to the same slide at minute 5 and minute 50, a global merge would fuse two distant moments into one token and destroy the timeline. Adjacent merging keeps each memory slot contiguous and ordered.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Latent actions: a controller learned from unlabelled video
question: A model's $\Delta_t\mathrm{PSNR}$ is close to 0. What does that tell you?
options: The video quality is very high
The tokenizer failed to reconstruct frames
The model is perfectly controllable
Random actions produce frames about as close to the truth as inferred actions, so the actions barely control the output
explain: If swapping the true latent actions for random ones does not change how far the prediction lands from the real frame, the model is mostly ignoring the action input. High controllability shows up as a large positive gap.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Turning an image into a sequence of patch tokens
question: In Hugging Face's `ViTForImageClassification`, which vector does the classifier read?
options: The average of all 197 output vectors
The output at the last patch position, like a decoder LLM
The final hidden state at position 0, the CLS token
A concatenation of all 196 patch outputs
explain: The source takes `sequence_output[:, 0, :]` (position 0 is CLS) and passes it to `self.classifier`, a single `nn.Linear(hidden_size, num_labels)`. Averaging patch outputs is a valid alternative design (global average pooling), but it is not what this class does.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Linear probe, LoRA or full fine-tune: choosing what to train
question: Your linear probe on frozen ViT features gets 91% on your validation set; full fine-tuning gets 90%. What does this most likely tell you?
options: Fine-tuning code has a bug, because FT always wins in distribution
The pretrained features already separate your classes well; fine-tuning (maybe with too high a learning rate or too little data) is not adding much
Linear probing is overfitting, since it has fewer parameters
You should switch to a larger patch size
explain: Probing is a strong baseline whenever the features are good, which is why CLIP reports it. FT usually wins slightly in distribution, but not always: with little data or an aggressive learning rate it can distort useful features. Try a lower learning rate, LLRD or LP-FT before concluding anything.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: pi0: denoising a whole action chunk with flow matching
question: Why does pi0 prevent the image and language tokens from attending to the state and noisy-action tokens?
options: So the prefix's keys and values stay valid across all 10 denoising steps and the prefix stays close to the VLM's pretraining
Because PaliGemma cannot process more than 256 tokens
To make the action expert bidirectional
Because flow matching requires a causal mask over time steps
explain: If the prefix could see the noisy actions, its keys and values would change every step and could not be cached. The paper also states the mask minimizes distribution shift from PaliGemma's pretraining.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Codebook collapse: measuring and fixing unused codes
question: A tokenizer with 1024 codes reports perplexity 1000 on one batch and 40 on another batch of the same size. What does that tell you?
options: The second batch's images use far fewer distinct codes, or a few codes dominate
The second batch had higher reconstruction quality
Perplexity is the cross-entropy of the transformer, so the second model is better
Nothing; perplexity is always equal to the codebook size
explain: Perplexity exp(H) of the code-frequency distribution is the effective number of equally used codes. 40 means the batch's tokens concentrate on roughly 40 codes' worth of entropy, which could be simple images or a collapsing codebook; compare across batches to tell which.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Token budgets: bits per image, 1D tokenizers and early fusion
question: TiTok-L-32 and a 16 x 16 VQGAN with 1024 codes both tokenize 256 x 256 images. How many bits per image does each use?
options: 384 bits and 2560 bits
32 bits and 256 bits
4096 bits and 1024 bits
12 bits and 10 bits
explain: TiTok: 32 tokens x log2(4096) = 32 x 12 = 384 bits. VQGAN: 256 tokens x log2(1024) = 256 x 10 = 2560 bits. TiTok uses about 6.7x fewer bits and 8x fewer tokens.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: KV cache layout and block sizes per backend
question: Which layout puts every KV head of one token next to each other inside a block?
options: LBHNC
LBNHC
LHBNC
BHLNC
explain: In LBNHC the order inside a block is N, then H, then C, so for a fixed token all heads are adjacent. LBHNC and BHLNC keep each head's tokens together instead, and LHBNC moves heads outside the block.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: What an image costs: provider token formulas and resizing rules
question: Using Claude's formula, how many tokens does a 560 x 280 image cost (no resizing needed)?
explain: $\lceil 560/28 \rceil \cdot \lceil 280/28 \rceil = 20 \cdot 10 = 200$. 784 is $28^2$, and 156,800 is the raw pixel count.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Herlihy's universal construction: announce, then help
question: A teammate removes the `help` lookup so each process always proposes its own cell. Which property is lost?
options: Linearizability: operations might be applied twice
Lock-freedom: the system might stop making progress
Wait-freedom: a slow process can lose every consensus round, though the system still progresses
Nothing: consensus still picks one cell per slot
explain: Each consensus round still threads exactly one cell, so the system progresses and nothing is applied twice. But nothing forces a slow process's cell to win, so that process can starve. Herlihy states this directly: without helping the protocol is non-blocking but not wait-free.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Rolling a 6-hour step out to 10 days
question: Using Pangu-Weather's greedy schedule with 24, 6, 3 and 1 hour models, how many model calls produce a 100-hour forecast?
options: 6 calls: four 24 h, one 3 h, one 1 h
5 calls: four 24 h and one 4 h
17 calls: all 6 h steps
100 calls: all 1 h steps
explain: 100 = 4 x 24 + 4. The 6-hour model does not fit into the remaining 4 hours, so the greedy loop uses one 3-hour and one 1-hour call: 4 + 1 + 1 = 6. There is no 4-hour model.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Foundation models, hybrids, and where these models break
question: A team has only 4 years of data for a new pollutant and wants global 5-day forecasts. Why is fine-tuning a pretrained Earth model like Aurora attractive?
options: The backbone already learned atmospheric dynamics from over a million hours of data, so only the new variables and mapping must be learned
Fine-tuning removes the need for any target data
Pretrained models do not need initial conditions
Fine-tuning guarantees beating CAMS on every target
explain: This is the foundation-model argument: the expensive dynamics are learned once. Aurora fine-tuned on limited CAMS analysis data (plus CAMS reanalysis) and matched or beat CAMS on 74% of targets, not all of them.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Production run queues: fixed rings, steal half, a LIFO slot
question: A task keeps waking a partner task, which wakes it back, forever. Without a cap, what goes wrong with the LIFO slot?
options: Nothing, both tasks get CPU time
The two tasks could take turns in the LIFO slot and starve everything in the local queue; Tokio disables the slot after 3 uses in a row
The tasks are stolen by other workers
The global queue overflows
explain: The LIFO slot always runs before the local queue. Two tasks ping-ponging through it would monopolize the worker, so Tokio disables it after 3 consecutive uses until a task from elsewhere runs.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Tuning the cooldown: length, shape, floor and data
question: Your WSD run uses a 2% linear cooldown, and the final model is noticeably worse than a cosine baseline of the same length. What is the most likely fix?
options: Raise the peak LR so the stable stage makes more progress
Skip the cooldown and use the last stable checkpoint
Switch the cooldown to an LR increase
Lengthen the cooldown to roughly 10 to 20% of training, or at least enough absolute steps
explain: A very short cooldown leaves the hill component frozen in place (MiniCPM: 2.5% falls short, 10% enough; Hägele: gains plateau near 20%). A higher peak LR would only raise the hill further.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: splice and tee: pipes as buffers of page references
question: A proxy splices 1 MiB from one socket to another through a pipe with the default capacity. Each splice moves a full pipe's worth. How many splice calls does it make?
explain: Default capacity is 16 pages, 65,536 bytes. 1,048,576 / 65,536 = 16 rounds, and each round is one splice into the pipe and one out of it: 32 calls. Two would need a 1 MiB pipe (settable with F_SETPIPE_SZ); 256 is the number of 4 KiB pages.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Embedding similarity with label descriptions
question: You rewrite all four label descriptions to be more specific. Which work must be redone?
options: Re-embed every input text and retrain the embedding model
Nothing; cosine similarity is unaffected by wording
Re-embed only the input texts
Re-embed the 4 label descriptions and re-tune the thresholds on labeled data
explain: Input embeddings do not depend on the labels, so they stay valid. The 4 label vectors must be recomputed, and because the cosine scale shifts with wording (bare names topped out at 0.31, descriptions at 0.52 in our example), any threshold has to be chosen again.
